questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: What AI can do today and what it still finds hard
How to become a chess champion with computer help
Why science fiction films about robots are popular
How computers are designed and built in factories
questions.why: Neil and Tim discuss where AI is used now and the limitations it still has.

questions.q: What does Tim think about AI at the start?
options: It is dangerous and should be stopped
It is already better than humans
It is still just science fiction
It is only used in hospitals
questions.why: Tim says there's a lot of talk about AI, 'but it's still just science fiction, isn't it?'

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an example Neil gives of AI in use today?
options: Helping us drive cars
Marking student essays
Finding out what's wrong with patients
Cooking meals at home
questions.why: Neil mentions driving, diagnosing in hospitals, marking essays and suggesting what to read, but not cooking.

questions.q: Why does Tim doubt that computers can solve real-life problems?
options: They are too slow
They think only in zeros and ones
They break down too often
They can't learn from mistakes
questions.why: Tim says computers think in zeros and ones, which sounds 'pretty limited' for life experience.

questions.q: According to the Cambridge professor, what is very difficult to get computers to do?
options: Play games like chess against the best human players
Do difficult maths problems very quickly
Remember large amounts of information for a long time
Simple things like walking or recognising a person
questions.why: He says things we take for granted, like walking, reaching or recognising our mother, are incredibly hard for computers.

questions.q: What does the professor say about these everyday tasks?
options: They are where the newest research is happening
They will never be possible for computers
They were solved many years ago
They are not important for AI
questions.why: He says 'that's where the current cutting edge of research is'.

questions.q: Why does Neil mention that a computer beat a chess grandmaster?
options: To prove computers are smarter than people in every way
To show a computer can win at chess but not pick up a piece
To explain how chess computers learn and plan their moves
To show that Tim is good at chess and often beats Neil
questions.why: Neil says the same computer would find it incredibly difficult to pick up a chess piece.

questions.q: How does Neil react when Tim says his quiz answer was an educated guess?
options: He agrees Tim knows a lot about chess
He says Tim must have cheated
He suggests Tim was maybe just lucky
He says the answer was wrong
questions.why: Neil replies, 'Or maybe you were just lucky'.
